messages:
carla_acme_sre: Hey team — our Redwood Private endpoints are flaky behind our corp proxy. Some clients get TLS handshakes with a cert for our internal gateway instead of Redwood, others get 502s. Started after we rolled a DNS change. Seen across multiple hosts in the same office.

priya_support: sorry to hear that, can you paste a curl/openssl trace and an example client IP? also did you change any egress allowlist entries? :thinking_face:

carla_acme_sre: quick repro from one of the affected hosts:

```
# using corporate proxy
curl -v -x http://corp-proxy:8080 https://public.private.redwood.example.com/ 2>&1 | sed -n '1,120p'
* Connected to corp-proxy (10.10.2.5) port 8080 (#0)
> CONNECT public.private.redwood.example.com:443 HTTP/1.1
> Host: public.private.redwood.example.com:443
> Proxy-Authorization: Basic REDACTED
>
< HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established
< Proxy-Agent: Acme-Proxy/4.2
* Proxy replied OK to CONNECT
* CONNECT phase completed
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Client hello (1)
*** server certificate does not match 'public.private.redwood.example.com'
*** Certificate chain
***
*** no peer certificate available
* closing connection 0
curl: (35) error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure
```

carla_acme_sre: but running openssl s_client directly to the same resolved IP (bypassing proxy) returns Redwood cert with CN=private.redwood.local. So looks like the CONNECT tunnel is getting intercepted after the proxy responds 200.

ben_infra: interesting — two possibilities: either the proxy is doing MITM (terminating and reissuing certs) or the CONNECT is being forwarded to an internal LB that doesn't SNI-match and returns generic gateway cert. you mentioned a DNS change — could the corp resolver be returning split-horizon answers for the hostname?

carla_acme_sre: yes we moved authoritative entries to our internal resolver for that subdomain. From affected host: `dig +short public.private.redwood.example.com @10.10.1.2` -> `10.20.30.40` (internal gateway). From a host that works (mobile tether): `52.45.12.3` (public).

alex_netops: ah. corp-proxy is likely in-path and doing SNI-based routing to that internal gateway. Because CONNECT binds raw TCP, proxies SHOULD tunnel and not rewrite SNI, but some enterprise proxies accept CONNECT then perform SNI steering or TLS interception. Two quick checks: 1) after CONNECT 200, run `openssl s_client -connect <proxy>:<tunnel-port> -servername public.private.redwood.example.com` and inspect the cert chain; 2) tcpdump on the client to see server IP post-CONNECT.

carla_acme_sre: ran tcpdump during the curl repro. After CONNECT 200, host opens TLS to 10.20.30.40 (internal gw). That gw returns a cert with CN=acme-gw.internal and a chain signed by corp root.

priya_support: that matches MITM. Two ways to move forward: a) ask your proxy/infosec to whitelist the Redwood public IPs or SNI so the CONNECT is pure tunnel; b) if whitelisting isn't possible, we can provide a customer-only hostname with a cert chain trusted by your corp PKI (not ideal). Also check whether your proxy rewrites the Host header — though for CONNECT it shouldn't.

ben_infra: additional thing to check: some proxies rewrite or inject ALPN or set up an upstream TLS session to the internal GW even after CONNECT. Could you capture the first bytes after the CONNECT? The openssl s_client with `-msg -tls1_3` will print client hello. If SNI in ClientHello is the public hostname but the proxy then proxies to an internal IP, the internal gw may present the wrong cert.

carla_acme_sre: here's the openssl extract:

```
openssl s_client -connect corp-proxy:8080 -proxy corp-proxy:8080 -servername public.private.redwood.example.com -tlsextdebug -status
# partial output
>>> TLS 1.3, ClientHello, .... tls extension server_name (len=26)
    ServerName: public.private.redwood.example.com
<<< ServerHello, TLSv1.3
<<< certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate
Certificate chain
 0 s:/CN=acme-gw.internal
   i:/CN=Acme-Root-CA
```

alex_netops: that shows the proxy is answering CONNECT and then doing TLS intercept. If your security policy forbids disabling MITM, you need to ensure the proxy forwards the original connection to the real redwood IP. The common fixes: update split-dns so internal resolver returns public IP for that host (so CONNECT goes to public infra), or add an egress allowlist for the public IPs and bypass MITM for that destination.

priya_support: from our side, we can also check if your account is pinned to a specific Redwood instance with a private IP. If so, we can expose a dedicated hostname that resolves only to our public endpoint IPs to make routing easier for your netops. I can open an internal ticket to see IP ranges used by Private endpoints.

carla_acme_sre: thanks. InfoSec says they can't disable TLS intercept globally, but can create proxy bypass rules for specific FQDNs if we provide a list of FQDNs/IPs. Priya — please send the current IPs and a recommended bypass list.

priya_support: will do. Also please collect these for each affected host and paste `traceroute -n public.private.redwood.example.com` and `dig +short public.private.redwood.example.com` outputs. If you want, we can schedule a short troubleshooting session with netops+support.

infra-bot: ticket #SUP-11472 created for IP whitelist request — assigned to priya_support, priority P2.

ben_infra: one last note — if your proxy does SNI rewriting rather than MITM, you may see mismatched cert CN but no corp root in chain. In your case chain is corp-root signed so it's true MITM. Ok next steps: priya to send redwood IP/netblocks, carla to collect traceroutes/dig across 3 hosts, netops to request bypass.

carla_acme_sre: will collect traces and follow up. thanks everyone :heart:
